items.stem: A code-review skill used by a 40-engineer platform team invokes a git rebase command it should never touch, and its dependency-scan output crowds review findings out of context before finishing, breaking the team's pre-merge SLA. Which two changes fix this? Select two.

opts.t: Scope `allowed-tools` in the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter to exclude the rebase command.
Set `context: fork` for the skill so the dependency scan runs isolated and only its result returns.
Add a `deny` rule for the rebase command to `settings.json` permissions, blocking it for every skill.
Add an instruction to the skill's body telling it never to run destructive git commands.

items.whyRight: Scoping `allowed-tools` removes the skill's access to the rebase command entirely, and `context: fork` isolates the dependency scan so only its result returns to the main conversation — each config axis is matched to the requirement it actually governs, independently of the other.

whyWrong.C: A `deny` rule blocks the command for every skill and tool project-wide; nothing here calls for restricting the whole project, only this one skill's own tool access.
whyWrong.D: Prose in the skill body asks the model to police itself and competes with everything else in context; it does not change what the skill is actually permitted to run.

items.t1Clause: invokes a git rebase command it should never touch (restricted to this one skill only)
items.factAnswerRaw: Scope `allowed-tools` in that skill's frontmatter; Set `context: fork`

items.stem: A team is migrating a deprecated HTTP client across 60 files with three viable sequencing strategies, each carrying a different risk of breaking existing integrations. A mid-migration reversal would cost a sprint's worth of rework. What level of process fits before starting?

opts.t: Begin the migration immediately using whichever file order seems fastest, adjusting course if an integration breaks.
Assign the migration to the most senior engineer instead of planning the sequence, trusting seniority to lower ordering risk.
Use plan mode to design and get sign-off on a sequencing strategy before touching any file, then execute directly.
Adopt a standing rule that every repository change, including single-file fixes, must go through a written plan and multi-team approval.

items.whyRight: Plan mode produces a reviewable sequencing plan before any file changes, matching the blast radius of a 60-file migration where a wrong order costs a sprint to reverse — sufficient process for the risk, without converting this migration into a standing rule for every future change.

whyWrong.A: Starting without a plan lets the sequencing choice get made ad hoc; by the time an integration breaks, reversing it costs the sprint the plan was meant to avoid.
whyWrong.B: Seniority does not resolve which sequencing order is safest across three viable strategies; that decision needs the deliberation plan mode provides, not a more experienced person working without one.
whyWrong.D: A 60-file migration justifies a plan; extending written approval to every future change, single-file fixes included, taxes routine work to control a risk that rarely exists elsewhere.

items.t1Clause: three viable sequencing strategies, each carrying a different risk

items.stem: A shared coding agent must never force-push, per a signed security policy, and its formatter must run after every file edit regardless of which engineer is driving the session. Which two configuration changes guarantee both, independent of any prompt wording? Select two.

opts.t: Add a strongly-worded instruction to the project's CLAUDE.md forbidding force-push and reminding the agent to run the formatter.
Escalate the rule to managed enterprise policy settings, even though only this one shared agent's configuration is affected.
Add a `deny` rule for the force-push command pattern to `settings.json` permissions.
Add a `PostToolUse` hook, scoped to file-edit events, that runs the formatter automatically.

items.whyRight: A `deny` rule blocks force-push outside model discretion, regardless of prompt wording, and a `PostToolUse` hook runs the formatter every time a file-edit event fires — both are enforced by Claude Code itself, not by instructions the agent could choose to weigh differently.

whyWrong.A: A CLAUDE.md instruction shapes what the agent tries to do; it does not change what Claude Code allows, so a determined or malformed prompt can still bypass it.
whyWrong.B: Managed policy fits a rule that must survive every local override across many machines; escalating one shared agent's rule there is more governance than this situation calls for.

items.factAnswerRaw: A `deny` rule in `settings.json` permissions; A hook on the relevant event, scoped by matcher

items.stem: A twelve-engineer partner team onboarded well via a live Claude Code setup walkthrough. Six weeks ago that walkthrough was recorded as a video and the live sessions retired; new partners' generated code has since missed conventions added afterward. What is the most direct fix?

opts.t: Publish a written FAQ answering common partner setup questions, updated whenever the setup team remembers to.
Re-record the walkthrough video today so it captures this quarter's conventions.
Give partners the version-controlled shared configuration itself, plus an onboarding path that stays current as it changes.
Have each new partner set up their own personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` mirroring the walkthrough's conventions.

items.whyRight: Version-controlled configuration and a living onboarding path update automatically as the setup evolves, so partners always receive the current conventions; a recorded walkthrough is frozen the moment it is made and confidently teaches whatever was true then, not what is true now.

whyWrong.A: A FAQ depends on someone remembering to update it and on partners finding the right page; neither is guaranteed the way a version-controlled artifact that ships with the repository is.
whyWrong.B: Re-recording fixes this quarter's gap but freezes again the moment it is published; the same drift recurs at the next convention change, on the same recorded-and-frozen failure mode.
whyWrong.D: Personal, user-level configuration is invisible in review and does not travel with a clone; the next new partner who joins still inherits none of it.

items.factAnswerRaw: Version-controlled shared configuration, skills and commands, plus an onboarding path they follow
